source.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
source.authors: J. Kaplan; Sam McCandlish; T. Henighan; Tom B. Brown; Benjamin Chess; R. Child; Scott Gray; A. Radford; Jeff Wu; D. Amodei

record.file_problem: The complete paper text is present. Some equations and figure content are flattened, but the relevant text results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: Measures held-out language-model loss and overfitting across model and dataset sizes, extending the study of generalization to autoregressive language models on WebText2.
record.gate_note: The paper reports natural-language test-loss and overfitting results, but does not test random-label fitting or the specific conditions in V1–V8. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures language-model scaling and data-limited overfitting, but none of V1–V8. Increasing total Transformer size with early stopping does not test widening beyond zero training error. Batch-size experiments measure steps and tokens required to reach target losses, without establishing a held-out performance penalty under a fixed epoch budget.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors report predictable power-law relationships between language-model loss, model size, dataset size, and training compute or steps. They conclude that larger models are more sample efficient and that compute-efficient training stops before convergence. They acknowledge poor fits in the smallest-data regime, unoptimized regularization, and uncertainty about theoretical foundations and extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: Autoregressive Transformer language modeling on natural text, with test cross-entropy and dataset-size scaling; no random-label experiment or image-classification setup.
record.method_sensitivity: Model and dataset size affect overfitting; the fitted relation is poor in the smallest-data regime. The authors did not optimize dropout while varying model and dataset size.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed dataset size, early-stopped test loss shows diminishing improvements as Transformer size increases; excess loss relative to the infinite-data reference grows predictably with model size relative to data size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transformer language-model test loss depends jointly on model and dataset size, with a data-limited plateau and predictable excess loss under the tested early-stopping and dropout recipe.

fits_no_version.finding: For 300M-parameter models, finite-data test-loss trajectories initially track unrestricted-data training before diverging; the train–test loss difference overestimates excess test loss relative to the infinite-data reference.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these language-model experiments, the train–test gap overestimates the performance penalty attributable to limited training data.

record.problems: The study reports no random-label condition. The smallest-dataset runs fit the joint model poorly, and the authors say they did not optimize regularization while varying dataset and model size. Some reported trends are described from figures without individual numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Figure-only details without numerical descriptions were not reconstructed as separate values.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and the paired natural-label versus random-label held-out comparison.
Width increases beyond the width achieving zero training error, with convergence and subsequent test-error measurement.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled adaptive-optimizer versus SGD comparisons and the effects of tuning or optimizer modifications.

Large-versus-small batch held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets and recipe changes that recover performance. Critical-batch-size and target-loss efficiency measurements do not establish this comparison.
Dropout versus no-dropout comparisons, dropout strength, and interactions with training-set size or augmentation.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with train–test gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Retraining after removal of highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The cannot_determine states concern the listed claim versions; they do not dispute the unrelated empirical findings. Section 7's discussion of interpolation transitions does not supply a zero-training-error width experiment. No version-specific verdict is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison of random-label and natural-label held-out performance.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep, interpolation threshold, or MNIST/downsampled CIFAR-10 experiment.
No convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier comparison.
No controlled comparison of adaptive optimizers with SGD on held-out performance.
No large-versus-small batch comparison of held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout is used in one experiment, but its effect is not compared against a no-dropout condition.
No sharpness or other trained-network property is measured against the train–test gap.

rows.check: The trend is reported, but cannot establish any listed version. The stage incorrectly imports near-convergence training on full WebText2 from Section 3.2; Figure 9 uses dataset subsets, 10% dropout, and early stopping. The stated size range is paper-wide, not established for this figure. Flattening of early-stopped loss should not be interpreted as worsening test loss with increasing size.
